:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="57381"}
I appreciate you telling me how you feel, and I want you to know I was asking you out of respect for you, not because I was looking for permission.

My honest answer to your question is yes. If the situation were reversed, I would be comfortable with you going because I trust you. For me, it comes down to trust rather than who else is there.

I wanted to include you in the decision because your feelings matter to me. That's why I asked in the first place. ❤️
:::

Your original message already shows respect. You didn't say, "I'm going." You asked first.

You could respond with something like this:

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="28416"}
I asked because I respect you and wanted to include you, not because I was hiding anything or asking for permission. My honest answer to your question is yes. If the roles were reversed, I would be completely comfortable with you going because I trust you.

I wasn't asking to test boundaries. I was asking because your feelings matter to me, and I wanted to make sure we were on the same page.
:::

I don't like this response from my bf about a friend happy hour I asked if I could go to out of reepse t for him: Been spraying killer after my sales call. Love ya & you do you. Just ask yourself would you be comfortable with me going there with a girl that had the same intention as Stewart? Like I said love, you do you. ❤️my answer would be yes

Is is accusatory or he's trying to teach me or what
This is what I wrote Hey babe, would it be okay if I went to Stewart's surprise birthday happy hour at North Italia with a large group of people?
Add in my response that I was asking him out of respect

Based only on that text, I don't read it as outright accusatory. I do think it's carrying a few different messages at once.

What stands out to me:

- **"Love ya & you do you."** This sounds like he's trying not to control you. He's explicitly saying the decision is yours.
- **"Just ask yourself would you be comfortable with me going there with a girl that had the same intention as Stewart?"** This is where he's communicating his discomfort. Rather than saying, "I don't want you to go," he's asking you to apply the situation to yourself.

That question does carry an assumption: that Stewart's intentions are romantic or inappropriate. If you don't agree with that assumption, then it can feel unfair or even a little manipulative because it frames the situation in a particular way.

If your genuine answer is, **"Yes, I'd be completely fine with that,"** then the comparison doesn't really work. It means the two of you may simply have different boundaries around opposite-sex friendships.

So I wouldn't describe his message as "teaching" you as much as **trying to get you to see the situation from his perspective**. Whether that's healthy depends on whether he's open to hearing that your perspective is different.

You could simply respond:

> "My honest answer is yes. If the situation were reversed, I would trust you. I appreciate that you shared how you feel, but for me it comes down to trust rather than who else is there."

That keeps the conversation focused on your different comfort levels instead of arguing about whether Stewart's intentions are or aren't what your boyfriend believes.

One question: Does your boyfriend have a specific history with Stewart that makes him think Stewart has those intentions, or is this just his general concern about male friends?
